title: Pensions and the 401(k)
headline: Who sold us the 401(k)?
question: In 1975 seven in ten workers in a retirement plan earned a pension. Now it’s one in ten. Who sold us the 401(k)?
intro: In 1975 seven in ten workers in a workplace retirement plan were earning a pension. By 2022 it was about one in ten. Move the idea through the people who carried it, from the pension as a promise to the 401(k) as an account.

stations.title: The first pension
stations.what: Creates the first private pension plan in the United States.
stations.pitch: A monthly check for life after a long career, paid for by the employer.

stations.title: Pensions go to the bargaining table
stations.who: The labor board and the courts; Inland Steel
stations.where: Inland Steel Co. v. NLRB, 1948 to 1949
stations.what: The courts uphold the labor board: pensions are something unions can bargain over. The Supreme Court declines to review it in 1949.
stations.pitch: Retirement pay is part of pay.
stations.spread: Unions can now put pensions on the table in contract talks.

stations.title: The Treaty of Detroit
stations.who: Walter Reuther, United Auto Workers; General Motors
stations.what: Trades labor peace for pensions, health care and cost-of-living raises.
stations.pitch: Long-term peace in exchange for long-term security.
stations.spread: Ford and Chrysler sign similar deals. Fortune magazine gives it its name.

stations.title: A promise breaks
stations.what: The plant closes and its pension plan fails.
stations.spread: More than 8,500 auto workers lose some or all of their promised benefits. It becomes the case for federal pension insurance.

stations.title: Insure the promise
stations.who: Sen. Jacob Javits; President Gerald Ford
stations.what: Sets federal rules for private pensions and creates the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation to insure them.
stations.pitch: No worker should lose a promised pension again.
stations.spread: Javits had pushed for pension reform since 1967. Ford signs it on September 2, 1974.

stations.title: A small tax rule
stations.what: Adds Section 401(k), a narrow tax rule for deferred pay, reportedly aimed at executives’ profit-sharing plans.
stations.pitch: Settle how deferred pay is taxed.
stations.spread: Its own champions later say it was never meant to be anyone’s main retirement plan.

stations.title: Accounts, not promises
stations.what: Argues for replacing Social Security with private accounts.
stations.spread: Cato hosts about 200 congressional staffers after Reagan’s election. The target is the public pension, not company plans.

stations.title: The 401(k) as we know it
stations.who: Ted Benna, benefits consultant; the IRS
stations.what: Benna sees a way for any worker to save from their own paycheck, with an employer match. IRS rules in November 1981 make it official.
stations.pitch: Easy saving, with free money from your employer.
stations.spread: 401(k)s spread through the 1980s while new pension plans all but stop forming.

stations.title: A long campaign
stations.who: Stuart Butler and Peter Germanis, Heritage Foundation
stations.what: A plan to build a coalition for private accounts over time.
stations.pitch: Build support for accounts, step by step.
stations.spread: Aimed at Social Security, not company pensions.

stations.title: Raiding the surplus
stations.who: Corporate raiders and employers; Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
stations.what: Overfunded pensions are shut down and the surplus taken back: over $20 billion since 1980, by the GAO’s count.
stations.pitch: The surplus belongs to the company.
stations.spread: Some of it helps pay for takeovers. Metzenbaum fights for a moratorium in 1988.

stations.title: A pension that looks like an account
stations.who: Kwasha Lipton, benefits consultants; Bank of America
stations.what: A pension designed to look like an account balance.
stations.pitch: Make the pension look like an account.
stations.spread: Kwasha Lipton sells the design to dozens of other employers.

stations.title: Tax the raids
stations.what: Puts a 10 percent tax on pension surplus taken back by employers, raised again in 1988 and 1990.
stations.pitch: Stop treating pension funds as piggy banks.

stations.title: The cash balance fight
stations.what: IBM’s switch to a cash balance plan is challenged as age discrimination.
stations.pitch: A new plan that treats every employee the same way.
stations.spread: A federal judge sides with the employees in 2003. IBM settles in 2004 and takes a $320 million charge.

stations.title: The ownership society
stations.what: Personal accounts at the center of Social Security reform.
stations.spread: Public disapproval of his handling rises from 48 to 64 percent, and the plan stalls.

stations.title: The freeze
stations.what: Companies with at least one frozen pension grow from 45 in 2004 to 237 in 2011.
stations.pitch: Cut costs and smooth out contributions.
stations.spread: Watson Wyatt finds most of the savings go into bigger 401(k) contributions.

stations.title: The 401(k) becomes the default
stations.who: Congress; Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi
stations.what: Encourages automatic enrollment and automatic increases in 401(k)s, building on their research.
stations.spread: Being in a 401(k) becomes the default at many employers.

stations.title: The father has regrets
stations.what: Says he regrets helping open the way for the financial industry, and that the 401(k) was never meant to be the main retirement plan.
stations.spread: He spends his later years working on plan fees.

stations.title: Where it landed
stations.what: 11.3 million workers actively earning a pension; 92.6 million in 401(k)-type plans.
stations.spread: In 1975, 71 percent of active plan participants were earning a pension. In 2022, 11 percent.

chart.note: Share of active participants in private-sector retirement plans who were in a defined benefit pension rather than a 401(k)-type plan, from Department of Labor Form 5500 data, 1975 to 2022. The department revised how it counts participants in 2004, so later years are not a perfect match for earlier ones. Before 1975 there is no comparable series.

findings.title: Never for everyone
findings.text: Even at the 1979 peak, only about half of private-sector workers had a retirement plan of any kind, according to Boston College’s Center for Retirement Research.

findings.title: The crossover
findings.text: In 1984, for the first time, more workers were active in 401(k)-type plans (30.5 million) than in pensions (30.1 million), by the Labor Department’s count.

findings.title: A slow fade, not a single kill
findings.text: The number of pension plans peaked at 175,143 in 1983 and fell to 46,508 by 2022. No one law ended them. Tax rules, consultants, raiders and boardrooms each moved them one step.

counterpoints.claim: A 401(k) moves with you. Workers who change jobs get noticeably smaller pensions, even when both employers have identical plans.
counterpoints.who: Boston College Center for Retirement Research

counterpoints.claim: A pension is only as good as the company behind it. Studebaker is why federal pension insurance exists.
